subtitle: Examine communication, feedback, decision-making and meeting practices on a diverse team. Check possible explanations with the people involved, then develop clear working agreements within agency responsibilities.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, managers, team leads and facilitators who lead culturally diverse teams and want system-level tools for norms, voice, decisions and accountability.

lessons.title: Examining team friction, working norms and assumptions
objectives: Identify the four common challenges of multicultural teams described by Brett, Behfar and Kern.
Describe the eight behavior scales of Erin Meyer's Culture Map and why positions on them are relative.
Separate observed behavior from possible cultural, structural or individual explanations for team friction.
Analyze a team conflict for the default working style it assumes.
lessons.teaching:
Leaders of diverse teams often meet friction that looks personal: one person seems blunt, another evasive, one keeps deferring to the supervisor, another challenges decisions in public. Cultural expectations and work structures are possible influences, alongside workload, unclear instructions, access barriers and individual circumstances. A framework cannot establish the cause of a particular conflict. In their 2006 article, Jeanne Brett, Kristin Behfar and Mary Kern identified four recurring challenges: direct versus indirect communication, trouble with accents and fluency, differing attitudes toward hierarchy and authority, and conflicting norms for decision-making. Their business-team analysis offers questions for examining working norms. It does not establish that culture explains a particular DHS employee’s conduct or that one intervention will work in every setting.

Erin Meyer's Culture Map offers a vocabulary for the same territory. It plots working styles along eight behavior scales: communicating, evaluating (how negative feedback is given), persuading, leading, deciding, trusting, disagreeing and scheduling. Meyer stresses that what matters is relative position. A person who seems very direct to one colleague may seem careful to another. The comparison invites questions about expectations. Do not assign colleagues positions from their names, backgrounds or a single interaction. This is a helpful correction to the common habit of treating one's own style as neutral and everyone else's as a deviation.

These frameworks come with the same cautions as any cluster research. Meyer's scales place national cultures by general tendency; Brett and colleagues describe patterns observed across many teams. None of it predicts an individual. On a DHS team, working styles are also shaped by profession, years in state service, disability and access needs, union and management roles, generation, and the organizational culture of the department itself. A leader who says "she is from that region, so she must be indirect" has turned a useful map into a stereotype.

Start with what happened and its effect on the work. Ask which expectations were explicit, what participants understood and whether the meeting format, workload or access arrangements contributed. A cultural explanation is a hypothesis to examine, not a substitute for hearing from those involved. When fast verbal debate is the unspoken norm, a leader may mistake quieter participation for disengagement. A team where decisions happen informally after meetings may frustrate people who expect the meeting to decide. Make working expectations explicit and offer usable ways to contribute. Concerns about threats, discrimination or other misconduct still need the appropriate response; do not defer required action while exploring communication styles.
lessons.keyPoint: Describe the behavior and its effect, then check possible explanations. Review working norms and access barriers without assigning a cultural profile or excusing misconduct.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: In a DSD project team, Marcus, a data analyst, openly challenges the project lead's timeline in weekly meetings. Nadia, a policy specialist, never disagrees in meetings but sends the lead careful emails afterward with concerns. Another member, Sione, tells the supervisor, Elena, that Marcus is "disrespectful" and Nadia is "not a team player." Elena notices the meetings are run as open debate, and decisions are treated as final by the end of each meeting.
lessons.question: What is Elena's most useful first step?
choices: Coach Marcus to be less confrontational and Nadia to speak up more, so both match the team's middle ground.

Examine the meeting format and ask participants what helps them raise concerns. Treat different disagreement styles as one possible explanation, and discuss usable ways to contribute before decisions are final.
Speculate with Sione about which cultural backgrounds explain Marcus's and Nadia's behavior.
feedback: Coaching individuals to a middle ground treats the problem as personal and leaves the structure unchanged. It may also cost the team the concerns both are raising.

This is the strongest response. Elena examines the observed pattern without deciding why Marcus or Nadia acts that way. She can clarify meeting expectations while addressing any separate conduct concern through the proper process.
Guessing colleagues' backgrounds and discussing them with a third person is stereotyping and could create a respectful workplace concern.
lessons.reflection: Using Elena’s fictional case, separate what she observed from what others inferred. What would she need to ask before attributing the pattern to culture?
lessons.action: At your next team meeting, observe how concerns reach the decision-maker. Note the format and one change you could propose, without assigning colleagues a cultural type.

check.question: Why does Erin Meyer emphasize relative position on her culture scales?
check.correct: Because how a style is perceived depends on the observer's own position; the same behavior can seem direct to one person and cautious to another.
wrong: Because every culture has a single correct position on each scale.
Because relative position lets leaders rank team members from most to least effective.
check.feedback: Relative position concerns how a behavior is perceived. The model does not rank effectiveness or establish an individual’s preferences, motives or cultural identity.

lessons.title: Communication and feedback across styles
objectives: Distinguish more explicit communication from communication that relies more on context and shared understanding.
Explain how upgraders and downgraders shape how negative feedback is heard.
Plan feedback practices that make expectations clear regardless of style.
Compare adapting to a colleague's style with imitating it.
lessons.teaching:
Communication styles vary in how much meaning is carried by the words themselves and how much by context, relationship and what is left unsaid. Some people and groups tend to say exactly what they mean and expect others to do the same. Others rely on shared understanding, tone and what is not said, and may find very explicit messages simplistic or even rude. The appropriate degree of detail depends on the task. Required instructions must be clear, even when people prefer different conversational styles. Problems arise when a team treats one pattern as the default and assumes everyone reads messages the same way.

Feedback is where this becomes most consequential for supervisors. Erin Meyer describes two sets of language tools. Upgraders, words like "absolutely" or "totally," strengthen criticism. Downgraders, words like "kind of," "sort of" or "a little," soften it. In her examples, a manager who used heavy downgraders was understood by a colleague from a more direct setting as offering a mild suggestion, when the manager meant that something had to change right away. Meyer also warns that people who try to imitate a much more direct style than their own can come across as aggressive. The goal is not to copy a style but to make sure the message lands.

For a supervisor in state service, the stakes are high. Performance expectations, coaching and formal feedback can affect a person's career. A message that one employee hears as clear direction and another hears as an optional idea is not a fair process. Practical safeguards include stating the level of importance plainly, whatever your style: "This is a required change" or "This is an idea to consider." Confirm expectations in an accessible format after the conversation. Invite the person to explain their understanding or use another workable way to check clarity; this is not a test of reading ability or accent. Balance positive and negative feedback over time. And learn how each team member prefers to receive feedback, asked of everyone as part of onboarding, not guessed from background.

Communication can also be affected by how listeners respond to accent or fluency. Accent alone does not establish language proficiency or job competence. Brett and colleagues list trouble with accents and fluency as one of their four challenges. In practice, people working in a second language may be interrupted, overlooked or judged on fluency rather than substance, while fluent speakers can dominate discussion. A leader can slow the pace, use pre-reads and written follow-ups, invite input in writing, and address any comments that mock accents or speech. Where a team member has a disability affecting communication, accommodation questions go through the ADA coordinator or the accommodation process. Formal performance processes follow HR policy and, where applicable, the collective bargaining agreement; your HR partner can advise.
lessons.keyPoint: Make the weight of feedback explicit no matter your style: say whether a change is required, confirm understanding and follow up in writing. Adapt to be understood, not to imitate.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Carmen, a DSD unit supervisor, tells a new case consultant, Oskar, that it "might be worth taking another look" at how he documents provider visits. She means the documentation does not meet requirements and must be fixed within two weeks. Oskar hears a small suggestion and moves on. A month later, an audit flags the same issue, and Carmen is frustrated that he ignored her. Oskar is surprised and upset.
lessons.question: What should Carmen do now?
choices: Start using stronger language with Oskar, since he seems to need blunt feedback.
Treat the missed message as Oskar's failure to listen and begin a formal performance process.

Acknowledge the unclear message, explain the documentation requirement and confirm an authorized deadline, support and accessible written follow-up. Consult the responsible audit and HR staff about required corrective steps.
feedback: Switching to a harsher style for one person risks seeming aggressive and still guesses at his preference instead of making the message clear.

The facts do not establish that Oskar ignored a clear instruction. Carmen should examine the communication and consult Human Resources about any required response. Clarifying feedback does not suspend audit, documentation or employment obligations.

This is the strongest response. Carmen corrects the ambiguity and confirms what is required without assuming a cultural cause. Any deadline or corrective process must fit the applicable requirements and her authority.
lessons.reflection: When you give critical feedback, what words do you use to soften or strengthen it? How might someone with a different style hear them?
lessons.action: Draft a sentence that distinguishes a required correction from optional advice. Plan an accessible way to confirm understanding, and follow the relevant documentation and HR process.

check.question: According to Erin Meyer, what is a risk of trying to imitate a much more direct feedback style than your own?
check.correct: You may come across as aggressive or harsh rather than clear.
wrong: Colleagues will always appreciate the extra clarity.
It guarantees that your message will be understood.
check.feedback: Meyer's examples show that imitation can backfire. A better approach is to keep your own voice while making the level of importance explicit and confirming understanding.

lessons.title: Hierarchy, voice and decision-making
objectives: Explain how attitudes toward hierarchy can affect whether team members speak up to a supervisor.
Distinguish decision norms that seek broad agreement from norms where a leader decides quickly, and the frustrations each can create for people used to the other.
Describe team psychological safety and its link to learning behavior.
Design decision rules and voice practices that do not depend on a single style of speaking up.
lessons.teaching:
Teams differ in how they relate to authority. In some working cultures, people expect to challenge the boss openly and see that as engagement. In others, people show respect by deferring to the person in charge, especially in public, and raise concerns privately or through someone else. In a state agency, these patterns meet a formal hierarchy of classifications, supervisors and managers, plus labor-management roles. A supervisor who says "my door is always open" may assume the invitation is enough. For some team members, speaking up to a supervisor in front of peers may feel inappropriate no matter how often they are invited.

Decision norms vary too, and deciding is one of the eight scales on Meyer's Culture Map. Some teams expect to reach broad agreement before a decision is made, which can take longer but brings people along. Others expect a leader to decide quickly and the group to adjust afterward. People used to one often misread the other. Someone expecting consensus may see a fast top-down decision as disrespectful; someone expecting a leader to decide may see a long consensus process as weak leadership. Brett and colleagues found that conflicting decision norms were a frequent source of friction in multicultural teams.

Team psychological safety connects these threads. Amy Edmondson defined it as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Her 1999 field study examined 51 teams in one manufacturing company. Psychological safety was associated with learning behavior, and the analysis linked learning behavior with performance. These findings do not establish that a particular meeting practice will cause better outcomes in DHS. Leaders can examine the conditions for participation without inferring a shared belief from silence or a single comment.

Practical designs help. Make decision rights explicit: for each type of decision, say who decides, who is consulted, and whether the decision is final or open to revision. Offer several ways to contribute, such as accessible written input, optional spoken turns and private follow-up. Explain who can access and retain responses. Do not promise anonymity unless the approved method supports it; details can identify someone even without a name. Ask for risks before deciding. Acknowledge useful concerns without naming or praising someone publicly against their wishes. Invite follow-up without requiring personal disclosure. Separate these team practices from formal channels: use the agency’s designated discrimination-reporting channels, including the Equal Opportunity and Access Division (EOAD); concerns about contract rights go through labor relations, and workplace conduct concerns go through HR.
lessons.keyPoint: Clarify who decides and how concerns can be raised. Examine substantive risks, protect information appropriately and check whether the available participation methods work for the team.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Terrence, a DSD section manager, leads a team that includes long-time staff and several recent hires from other states and countries. At a planning session he asks, "Any objections?" and hears none, so the plan moves forward. A week later, a recent hire, Anjali, tells a peer she saw a serious problem with the plan's data source but felt it was not her place to contradict the manager in front of senior staff. The peer passes this along to Terrence.
lessons.question: What should Terrence change first?
choices: Change how decisions are made: send proposals ahead with a written comment option, ask specifically for risks before deciding, state when a decision is final, and follow up on Anjali's point about the data source.
Tell Anjali privately that she needs to be more confident about speaking up in meetings.
Announce to the team that everyone must voice objections in meetings from now on.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Terrence should examine the data concern promptly with the responsible staff and explain whether the plan needs revision. He can improve routes for input without exposing a private conversation or claiming that one change establishes trust.
Putting the burden on Anjali treats her style as the problem and ignores why the meeting format did not surface a serious risk.
A rule requiring spoken objections reinforces a single style and may make people who prefer other routes less likely to contribute.
lessons.reflection: On your team, who speaks up in meetings, and whose views do you mostly hear another way or not at all? What in the structure might explain the difference?
lessons.action: For one decision your team will make this month, write down who decides, who is consulted, how input can be given in writing, and whether the decision is final or open to revision. Share it with the team before the meeting.

check.question: How did Amy Edmondson define team psychological safety?
check.correct: A shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.
wrong: A policy that guarantees no one will ever disagree in meetings.
An individual's personal confidence about speaking in groups.
check.feedback: The definition concerns a shared team belief. The study found associations with learning behavior; it does not let a supervisor diagnose the team from one person’s silence or guarantee an outcome from a meeting technique.

lessons.title: Time, trust and team agreements where no single style is the default
objectives: Compare task-based and relationship-based approaches to building trust, and linear and flexible approaches to scheduling.
Design a team agreement that makes working norms explicit and adjustable.
Plan how to review team agreements over time and hold the team, including the leader, accountable to them.
Identify which team concerns belong in formal channels rather than in a team agreement.
lessons.teaching:
Two more scales complete the picture. On trust, some people build it mainly through doing reliable work together: you trust me because I deliver. Others build it mainly through personal relationship: you trust me because we have come to know each other. On time, some people treat schedules and deadlines as fixed commitments, while others treat them as flexible and responsive to relationships and changing circumstances. On a DHS team, these differences can show up as frustration over meeting start times, over whether small talk is wasted time, or over when a deadline is truly a deadline.

Leaders need to set clear, lawful expectations while examining whether familiar methods create avoidable barriers. Some standards are required; other working arrangements can be developed with the team. Brett and colleagues describe four strategies for multicultural teams: adaptation, where members acknowledge cultural gaps and work around them; structural intervention, changing how the team is organized; managerial intervention, setting norms early or bringing in a higher-level manager; and exit, removing a member when other options fail. This business framework does not authorize a public employee’s removal. Employment actions require the applicable authority, HR and labor-relations processes, and procedural protections. Do not make employment decisions from cultural profiles. Urgent safety or conduct concerns may require prompt action through the appropriate process. The most useful everyday tools are the first three, and a team agreement is where they come together.

Invite team input on arrangements the team can influence and identify which requirements are already set. The resulting agreement names working expectations: how meetings start and end and what happens when someone joins late; which deadlines are fixed by law, contract or leadership and which are working targets; how feedback is given and how importance is signaled; how disagreement is raised, including written and private routes; who decides what; and how the team builds relationships, such as a brief check-in at the start of meetings that people can join or skip. The agreement should respect what the team cannot change on its own, such as hours, telework and scheduling provisions set by HR policy and collective bargaining agreements, and accommodation processes led by the ADA coordinator.

Accountability makes the agreement real. Review it at set intervals and when the team changes. Invite feedback through approved methods and explain access and privacy limits. An unnamed response is not necessarily anonymous. Ask what helps or creates barriers, and do not treat increased speaking as proof of psychological safety. Leaders should hold themselves to it first, because a supervisor who ignores the agreement signals that it applies only to others. Erin Meyer's advice fits here: expect the work to be hard, look at your own style from others' positions, find the value in other approaches, and keep adjusting. A team agreement is a living tool, not a finished product.
lessons.keyPoint: Design team agreements that make norms for time, trust, feedback, disagreement and decisions explicit. Build them together, review them regularly, hold leaders to them first, and respect formal HR, labor and accommodation processes.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Kofi, a DSD manager, has combined two units into one team. One group is used to starting meetings exactly on time and moving straight to the agenda. The other begins with ten minutes of check-in and treats internal deadlines as flexible when partner relationships need attention. Tension is growing, and one person, Bridget, has asked Kofi to just "set a rule" so everyone works the same way. A union steward has also mentioned that some staff have questions about schedule changes.
lessons.question: What should Kofi do?
choices: Set a rule matching the group that seems most efficient, since a clear standard is fairer.
Let each subgroup keep its own norms and avoid the issue, since both styles are valid.

Facilitate a team agreement that names which deadlines are fixed and which are working targets, how meetings open and when the agenda starts, and how disagreement is raised, while taking the schedule questions to HR and labor relations.
feedback: A common standard may be necessary, but apparent efficiency alone does not establish that it is appropriate or accessible. Kofi should explain fixed requirements, examine the work and consult the responsible partners on scheduling questions.
Avoiding the issue keeps the tension and leaves new members guessing which norms apply.
This is the strongest response. Kofi makes expectations explicit through a shared process, blends both needs where possible, and sends questions that involve employment terms to the right partners.
lessons.reflection: How do you tend to build trust at work: mainly through reliable work, mainly through relationship, or a mix? How might a colleague with a different approach read your behavior?
lessons.action: Draft three questions to open a team agreement conversation: one about time, one about trust and relationship, and one about how disagreement is raised. Schedule the conversation and plan a date to review what the team agrees.

check.question: Which of Brett, Behfar and Kern's strategies involves setting norms early or bringing in a higher-level manager?
check.feedback: Managerial intervention involves a leader setting expectations or becoming involved. Structural intervention changes how a team is organized. The framework’s exit category does not authorize employment action; applicable HR, labor-relations and procedural requirements govern.

cards.back: Brett, Behfar and Kern's list: direct versus indirect communication, accents and fluency, attitudes toward hierarchy, and conflicting decision-making norms.
Erin Meyer's scales: communicating, evaluating, persuading, leading, deciding, trusting, disagreeing and scheduling. Positions are relative, not absolute.
Words that can strengthen or soften criticism. Their effect depends on context and the listener; state required expectations explicitly and check understanding.
A shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.
Explicit working arrangements developed with team input, within agency authority and employment requirements, and reviewed as needs change.

aid.heading: Examine before judging
items: Describe what happened and its effect. Consider cultural expectations alongside workload, clarity, access and other possible explanations.
Identify the team's current default and who designed it.
Look for structures, such as meeting format or decision rules, that reward one style.
Never guess a colleague's background or explain behavior by a presumed culture.

aid.heading: Design for more than one style
items: State required expectations clearly and confirm understanding in an accessible format.
Make decision rights explicit: who decides, who is consulted, and whether it is final.
Offer usable written, spoken or private routes. Explain access and retention; promise anonymity only when the approved process supports it.
Ask for risks and the strongest counterargument before deciding.
Use pre-reads and a steady pace to support people working in a second language.

aid.heading: Keep agreements accountable
items: Invite input on the arrangements the team can change, identify fixed requirements and set a review date.
Hold leaders to the agreement first.
Ask what is working and what creates barriers, with clear privacy limits and no required personal disclosure.
Send discrimination concerns to EOAD, schedule and contract questions to HR and labor relations, and accommodation to the ADA coordinator.

sources.title: Harvard Business Review — Brett, Behfar and Kern, Managing Multicultural Teams (2006)
sources.note: Business-team framework retained as background. Public publisher preview and the authors’ abstract in PubMed were checked, including the four intervention categories. Full article access was unavailable; this is not a full methodological appraisal or authority for personnel action.

sources.title: Harvard Business Review — Erin Meyer, Navigating the Cultural Minefield (2014)
sources.note: Historical framework reference. Public preview checked; the author’s open discussion and tool guide separately support relative comparisons and eight dimensions. National tendencies are not individual profiles.

sources.title: INSEAD Knowledge — Erin Meyer, Giving Negative Feedback Across Cultures
sources.note: Author’s examples of feedback language and the risk of imitating directness. These examples do not establish universal preferences for any nationality.

sources.title: Harvard University — Edmondson, Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams (1999)
sources.note: University repository abstract checked: 51 teams in one manufacturing company, with associations among psychological safety, learning and performance. Full-paper or causal intervention review is not claimed.

sources.title: University of California, Berkeley, Department of Statistics — David A. Freedman, The Ecological Fallacy
sources.note: Supports the caution that group-level patterns, such as national scale placements, do not predict individual team members.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Equity Policy (2023)
sources.note: Department commitment to operate as an antiracist, multicultural and intercultural organization and to examine personal beliefs and biases, which frames leaders' responsibilities in this course.

sources.title: Erin Meyer — Mapping out Cultural Differences on Teams
sources.note: Author’s open account of relative comparisons. The course does not adopt national profiles as individual predictions or personnel criteria.

sources.title: Erin Meyer — Team Culture Map Help Guide
sources.note: Author’s tool guide identifies the eight dimensions. This course does not administer that assessment or assign profiles to coworkers.
